story_report.summary: Lindsay Clancy is scheduled to be retried on March 29, 2027, after her first trial over the deaths of her three children ended in a mistrial because jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict. Prosecutors are seeking a murder conviction, while Clancy’s lawyers contend that postpartum psychosis left her unable to control her behavior. The retrial will give a new jury the task of assessing competing accounts of her mental state and intent.

sections.heading: First Jury Deadlocked on Insanity
sections.body: Clancy has not disputed killing her three children in Duxbury in January 2023. According to accounts of the first trial, 11 jurors favored finding her not criminally responsible by reason of insanity, while one juror disagreed, preventing the unanimous decision required. Prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy had mental-health problems but argued that she acted deliberately and knew her actions were wrong.

sections.heading: Judge Sullivan Rejects Dismissal Request
sections.body: The defense sought dismissal, arguing that the court should have removed the juror who favored conviction and permitted deliberations to continue. Judge Sullivan ruled that the deadlock created a “manifest necessity” for a mistrial and that trying Clancy again would not violate double-jeopardy protections. Sullivan also found that further inquiry into deliberations and the requested juror-related records would improperly intrude on jury secrecy and would not be material to a retrial.

sections.heading: Retrial Planning Continues Before March
sections.body: Sullivan set the March 29 date after prosecutors sought a May trial date because of scheduling conflicts. Attorneys are due back in court on December 30, 2026, to address trial logistics, security and media arrangements. Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said prosecutors were ready to select a jury-trial date; defense lawyer Kevin Reddington said he took that as a sign prosecutors intend to pursue first-degree murder charges.

event_overview.title: About AI Safety
event_overview.subject: AI Safety
event_overview.summary: AI safety is the field of research, engineering, governance, and risk management concerned with ensuring that artificial-intelligence systems are reliable, secure, and used in ways that avoid serious harm. It encompasses immediate harms such as fraud, cyber misuse, and flawed automated decisions, as well as debated longer-term risks from increasingly capable general-purpose or autonomous systems. The September 2026 developments reflect a continuing policy and industry dispute over how quickly advanced AI should be developed and what safeguards should be required.

facts.label: Focus
facts.value: International assessments commonly focus on general-purpose AI systems—models that can perform a wide variety of tasks—and on emerging risks associated with frontier capabilities.

facts.label: Risk categories
facts.value: The 2026 International AI Safety Report groups major concerns into malicious use, malfunctions, and systemic risks; examples include cyber and biological misuse, unreliable or autonomous behavior, labor-market effects, manipulation, and potential loss-of-control scenarios.

facts.label: Industry safety practices
facts.value: Leading AI developers have adopted voluntary frontier-risk frameworks that use capability evaluations, thresholds, safeguards, incident reporting, and governance reviews before or during deployment. Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy and OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework are examples, not universal standards.

facts.label: Government and international coordinatio
facts.value: The United Kingdom convened the first AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park on November 1-2, 2023; participants backed the Bletchley Declaration and development of an independent scientific report on frontier-AI risks. The resulting International AI Safety Report series is intended to inform policymaking, rather than itself impose binding rules.

facts.label: Regulatory context
facts.value: AI-safety governance combines voluntary practices with binding rules in some jurisdictions. In the European Union, the AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024; governance rules and obligations for general-purpose AI models applied from August 2, 2025, while other provisions follow later timelines.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows a set of September 2026 statements, corporate disclosures, policy responses, and litigation-related developments; it does not constitute a complete history of AI safety research, regulation, or every AI-related incident.

event_overview.title: About Nvidia Scandal
event_overview.subject: Nvidia Scandal
event_overview.summary: “Nvidia scandal” is an informal label for a November 2026 corporate-governance and U.S. national-security controversy involving Nvidia, allegations concerning former chief executive Jensen Huang, and scrutiny of U.S. approvals for advanced AI-chip exports to China-linked buyers. It is not the name of a single formal court case or government proceeding: Nvidia’s public filing confirms Huang’s resignation and leadership transition, while lawmakers and administration officials have raised separate questions about export-control oversight and alleged diversion risks.

facts.label: Corporate transition
facts.value: Nvidia’s board accepted Jen-Hsun (Jensen) Huang’s resignation as president, chief executive officer and board member effective November 11, 2026; it appointed CFO Colette M. Kress interim CEO while it searches for a permanent successor.

facts.label: Company and location
facts.value: Nvidia is a Nasdaq-listed U.S. company; its November 12, 2026 leadership announcement was issued from Santa Clara, California.

facts.label: Export-control authority
facts.value: The U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) administers the relevant semiconductor-export licensing policy. On January 13, 2026, BIS said applications to export Nvidia H200 chips and similar products to China would be reviewed case by case when specified security conditions are met.

facts.label: Congressional scrutiny
facts.value: On November 12, 2026, the ranking members of the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees requested preservation of Commerce Department records concerning Nvidia export-license applications and communications involving Nvidia and Huang. The letter describes allegations and requests records; it is not a finding of wrongdoing.

facts.label: Policy issue at stake
facts.value: The controversy centers on whether controls and due diligence were adequate to prevent advanced U.S. AI chips from reaching unauthorized Chinese end users or being diverted through intermediaries, rather than on a settled legal determination about the allegations involving Huang or any customer.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major November 13-14, 2026 developments in the political and corporate fallout, but does not by itself establish the truth of espionage-related allegations, resolve any export-control inquiry, or cover every subsequent investigation or legal claim.

highlights.title: Congolese Politician Beaten After Promoting Ebola Awareness
highlights.summary: Marie-Celestin Karondwa, a politician from the ruling UDPS party in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, was beaten on Sunday after advocating for Ebola awareness during a radio interview. The incident occurred in Butembo, a region experiencing an Ebola outbreak, as residents reacted violently to his message promoting disease prevention measures.

The UK government has confirmed the evacuation and stated that established procedures are in place for handling such cases.

event_overview.title: About Awareness Outbreak
event_overview.subject: Awareness Outbreak
event_overview.summary: “Awareness Outbreak” refers to the 2026 Ebola disease emergency caused by Bundibugyo virus, centered in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and managed through national and international public-health response systems. Declared in May 2026, it has involved cross-border preparedness and imported-case responses in neighboring countries, while community engagement, testing, contact tracing and safe-care measures have been central to efforts to interrupt transmission.

facts.label: Start and international status
facts.value: The DRC declared the outbreak on 15 May 2026; WHO determined it to be a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, activating international coordination under the International Health Regulations.

facts.label: Disease involved
facts.value: The event concerns Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus (Bundibugyo virus disease), rather than the more common Ebola Zaire virus. WHO states that there was no approved vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo virus disease; care and control relied principally on early detection, isolation, supportive care and public-health measures.

facts.label: Geographic focus
facts.value: The outbreak began in northeastern DRC, with Ituri Province the epicentre, and expanded across multiple DRC provinces. WHO also documented cross-border spread or preparedness needs, including Uganda; Kenya later reported an imported case linked to travel from the DRC.

facts.label: Response leadership and methods
facts.value: DRC and Ugandan health authorities activated emergency coordination and response operations with WHO and partners. Core measures include surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical management, contact tracing, safe burials, cross-border coordination and community engagement.

facts.label: Why public awareness is material
facts.value: WHO identifies community engagement as essential to controlling this outbreak, particularly given insecurity, displacement, mobile populations and barriers to timely detection and access to care in affected areas.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline highlights particular late-September and October 2026 developments—especially awareness efforts, laboratory capacity, mortality reporting, and Kenya’s imported-case response—but it does not constitute a complete epidemiological record of the wider DRC-centered outbreak or every affected country.
